Here is my musical journey thus far:

I would say my musical taste has evolved throughout my life. I don't recall really giving a crap about music as a kid. I'm sure I enjoyed some stuff, but didn't seek music out. Then in my early teens, when I was in junior high school, I started paying a bit more attention to music, and actually seeking it out, and exploring it. I guess like most teenagers, I was looking for something to identify with. I am a little embarrassed to admit that the first album that I ever bought was Korn's Follow the Leader. I guess the blending of genres (in this case metal/rap) appealed to me. I had been hearing plenty of metal and punk (lots of Napalm Death, D.R.I., Dead Kennedys, Gwar, Angry Samoans, Carcass, Ramones, etc.) coming from my brother's room at that point, and it had started to grow on me. I had also started to dabble in graffiti at this time, and had been exposed to hip hop through that. It's no wonder why this blend appealed to me. I listened to a lot of crappy nu-metal during this time.

As I moved into my mid-late teens, I got more into graffiti, and hip hop, which I subsequently started exploring more thoroughly. That's when I discovered artists like Aesop Rock, Atmosphere, El-p, Non Phixion, Typical Cats, Hieroglyphics, etc. These days some of you may have heard of some, if not all of those, but at the time none of them were that popular/known, and I only discovered them through some internet exploration. As the internet became even more prevalent in the following years, and evolved, it became easier to find such artists, because whole sites dedicated to underground hip hop popped up. Anyway, I had also started exploring metal and, more so, punk a little further, and going to local shows, so my appreciation for that seemingly opposite (there is actually quite a bit of overlap between hip hop and punk) end of the genre spectrum also grew.

Then in my late teens-early 20s my musical appreciation really blossomed, and I discovered that I could find something to appreciate about most music. I think hip hop had a lot to do with this, as it is typically pretty sample heavy, and I started to question where these samples originated, which led me to other genres, such as jazz, blues, and electronic music. I also realized that thrash is my favourite form of metal, and hardcore my favourite form of punk, and that crossover is the combination of those two, and so that also became one of my favourite sub-genres.

From there, my taste has basically just expanded. But these days I listen mostly to hip hop, metal, punk, electronic music, and I guess what you could call "alternative rock" (Faith No More, Primus, Butthole Surfers, etc.). I'm always looking for new/different stuff though.

TL;DR:

My musical journey: nu-metal -> hip hop/punk/metal -> hip hop/punk/metal/electronic/"alternative" rock/anything that sounds good to me

As a child develops, a tug of war between genes and environment settles the issue of the child's intelligence. One theory on how that struggle plays out proposes that among advantaged kidsâ€”with the pull of educational resourcesâ€”DNA largely wins, allowing genetic variation to settle smarts. At the other end of the economic spectrum, the strong arm of poverty drags down genetic potential in the disadvantaged.

But over the years, researchers have gone back and forth on this theory, called the Scarr-Rowe hypothesis. It has held up in some studies, but inexplicably slipped away in others, leaving researchers puzzled over the deciding factors in the nature-vs-nurture battle. Now, researchers think they know why.

In a new meta-analysis of 14 psychology studies from the past few decades, researchers found that the strength of povertyâ€™s pull differed by country, with US poverty providing the only forceful yank among developed nations. The authors, who published the results in Psychological Science, speculate that the wider inequalities in education and medical access in the US may explain povertyâ€™s extra power. The finding could not only resolve the data discrepancies of the past, but it may also lead researchers to a more nuanced understanding of povertyâ€™s effects on IQ and how to thwart them.
